frameworks.name: Stone Cutter Perspective Frame
frameworks.definition: Three stone cutters doing identical work hold three distinct perspectives (complaint, subsistence, cathedral-building); the work itself is the same but meaning varies by frame.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that almost all businesses are fundamentally the same when abstracted two or three levels up, because at that level every business has a director of sales, director of marketing, director of IT, HR, and legal concerns that will be challenging on a recurring basis. He uses this as a reframe against the idea that a founder must love their specific industry to succeed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When you abstract far enough up, the operational complexity of running a business converges on the same set of functional problems regardless of industry, so the industry itself is not load-bearing for happiness or success.
bounded_by: May not apply to hyper-specialized technical businesses where domain expertise is the primary value driver

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business owner's goal should be to let the business be an expression of the values they hold rather than expecting the business to fill an emotional void (what he calls 'filling a hole in your heart'). He frames passion for the product or industry as an unreliable motivational engine compared to passion for excellence or craft.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi diagnoses a boat membership business at $2M revenue / $600K net profit (30% net margin) with $2M in debt as having a demand constraint rather than a margin or model constraint. The boat fleet (50 boats) creates a capital-intensive fixed cost base, but once those costs are covered each incremental membership produces disproportionately higher profit because the marginal cost of an additional member is near zero.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: subscription membership business with high fixed asset costs and near-zero marginal delivery cost per additional member
claims.mechanism: Fixed costs (fleet, facilities, licensing fees) are already absorbed at current membership count; each new member's revenue flows predominantly to profit with minimal incremental cost, making revenue growth disproportionately profitable.

numbers.axis: net profit margin for a boat membership business at $2M revenue

anchors.region: incremental member beyond fixed cost coverage
anchors.value: disproportionately high profit contribution per dollar of membership revenue

bounded_by: Applies only when fixed costs are already covered; early-stage before full fleet utilization would show lower incremental margins

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a 4% lead-to-close rate in a business where industry standard is 6% is not a signal of a broken sales motion or offer problem. He holds that industry benchmarks set by average operators are irrelevant because average operators are financially unsuccessful, and the correct diagnostic is whether the close rate points to a sales motion issue or an offer issue rather than whether it beats the industry average.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses using external marketing benchmarks as performance targets
claims.mechanism: Industry averages are pulled down by the majority of operators who are not profitable; a 4% close rate with strong unit economics ($5,000 initiation + $500/month) and acceptable lead costs ($11/lead) does not indicate a structural problem.

numbers.axis: lead-to-close rate benchmarks for boat membership businesses

anchors.region: business in question (with paid sales staff)

bounded_by: Close rate matters when lead cost is too high or when lead-to-close rate indicates a systematic objection not being overcome

claims.text: Alex Hormozi calculates that a lead cost of $11 and a close rate of 4% yields a customer acquisition cost (CAC) of approximately $266 before sales commissions for a boat membership business. He frames this as acceptable given a $5,000 initiation fee and $500/month recurring membership, concluding that the business has strong unit economics and the correct growth lever is more ad spend, not model changes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: At 4% close rate, 25 leads are needed per sale; 25 x $11 per lead = $275 in media cost, adjusted to ~$266 after rounding; this CAC is recouped within the $5,000 initiation fee making payback period less than one month.

numbers.axis: customer acquisition economics for a boat membership business

bounded_by: CAC figures exclude sales commissions; true CAC with commissions would be higher

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies a psychological pattern he calls 'exhale behavior' in business owners: they spend on marketing until they cover fixed costs and reach modest profitability, then stop spending and exhale in relief. He argues this is irrational because the marginal return on incremental marketing spend beyond the exhale point is high, and owners are effectively working hard to pay everyone else (landlord, licensor, employees) while forgetting to pay themselves via profit maximization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses with significant fixed cost bases
founder still involved in daily operations
claims.mechanism: Business owners cognitively anchor to the pain of near-zero or negative profit; once above that threshold their loss-aversion drops and marginal marketing investment stops even though the return on that investment remains high.
bounded_by: Does not apply when supply constraint limits capacity to serve additional customers; in that case increasing marketing without solving supply creates promise-delivery gap

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for a boat membership business at $2M revenue with 30% net margins and strong unit economics, the primary growth lever is increasing ad spend on Google AdWords combined with better creative and improved conversion rate optimization (CRO) on the funnel, not changing the business model or exiting the business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: strong unit economics (high initiation fee + monthly recurring)
claims.mechanism: When lead cost is acceptable and unit economics are strong, revenue growth is primarily gated by volume of leads, which scales with ad spend on validated channels. CRO improvements multiply the return on each ad dollar without requiring more spend.

numbers.axis: current ad spend for a $2M revenue boat membership business

anchors.value: significantly higher; amount unspecified but described as going hard

bounded_by: Only valid when supply (boat capacity, staff) can absorb additional member volume; would not apply if fleet is near capacity utilization

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that a 33% referral rate from existing members is a meaningful but juice-able acquisition channel that can be structured more formally to drive additional growth, noting that a structured referral system can be optimized beyond its current level.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: existing member base generating organic referrals

numbers.axis: new member source mix for a boat membership business

claims.text: Alex Hormozi frames a licensing fee of $30/month per member on a $500/month membership (6% of revenue, ~20% of margin) as non-strangling but material. He notes that framing it as a percentage of margin rather than percentage of revenue changes how burdensome it feels, and concludes it is not a reason to exit the business or consider the model broken.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: licensing model with per-member flat fee

numbers.axis: licensing fee burden at different denominators for a $500/month boat membership

bounded_by: Assessment assumes 30% net margin; at lower margins the licensing fee becomes more structurally burdensome

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a sales close rate is 10% when the founder does the selling but drops to 4% with a paid sales team, this is an expected and normal performance decay rather than a broken sales process, because founders outperform replacements as a structural rule.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder who previously handled all sales transitions to hired sales staff

numbers.axis: close rate by who is selling in a boat membership business

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the diagnostic framework for a stalled business is to check whether the constraint is demand (too few leads) or supply (too little capacity), and that the correct interventions differ sharply. In this case he diagnoses a demand constraint and prescribes increased ad spend rather than operational restructuring.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: sales motion issue or offer issue
claims.mechanism: If the close rate is acceptable and lead costs are acceptable, then growth is gated by lead volume (demand constraint); if close rate is low despite volume, the constraint is sales motion or offer (not demand).
bounded_by: Supply constraint analysis must precede demand investment; scaling demand into capacity-constrained delivery creates unfulfillable promises

examples.text: Alex Hormozi described a friend who transitioned from the fitness industry into running a gourmet cookie company before the crumble cookie trend emerged. The friend was not passionate about cookies but identified a gap in the market for high-end gourmet cookies. He tested approximately 100 recipes to find the best chocolate chip cookie, found the right one, and built a successful business. The business ultimately failed due to a bad partnership rather than market fit issues. Hormozi uses this story to illustrate that passion for the specific product is not required for business success; what matters is passion for excellence and identifying real market gaps.

Alex Hormozi walks through the unit economics of the boat membership business live during the session. The business charges a $5,000 initiation fee plus $500/month on 5-year contracts. Marketing costs $11/lead. At a 4% close rate, 25 leads are required per sale, yielding a media-only CAC of approximately $266. The initiation fee alone ($5,000) recovers CAC within the first payment, making it a very favorable acquisition model. Hormozi concludes the model is not broken and the right move is to scale ad spend rather than change the offer or exit.

During the session, Alex Hormozi describes how the boat membership founder had previously sold memberships personally at a 10% close rate, then transitioned to a paid sales team which closes at 4%. The founder arrived at the workshop believing this was a sign the offer or model was broken. Hormozi reframes the 4% close rate not as a problem to solve through offer changes but as expected performance decay from founder to hired staff, and notes the correct intervention is to increase volume of leads rather than improve close rate since the unit economics remain strong.

practices.text: Before accepting that an industry is wrong for you, reframe the business two to three levels up and ask whether the universal skills you are building (sales, marketing, ops, finance, HR) are valuable independent of the specific product or industry.

Calculate your true customer acquisition cost by dividing your cost per lead by your close rate, then compare it to your first-payment revenue. If the first payment recovers CAC, you have strong unit economics and should prioritize volume growth over model changes.

When diagnosing a business that is profitable but not growing, ask: is this a demand problem (not enough leads) or a supply problem (can't serve more customers)? Solve supply constraints before spending more on demand.

For Google AdWords-driven service businesses, test more and better creative and review keyword targeting before increasing budget; improve conversion rate optimization on the funnel to get more output per ad dollar before scaling spend.

Evaluate a licensing fee as a percentage of margin rather than a percentage of revenue to get the true impact on business economics; 6% of revenue on a 30% margin business is equivalent to 20% of margin and should be factored into exit or scale decisions accordingly.
